title: Reporting the sample and the data
summary: A results section starts with who the data come from, how many cases were analysed and how missing values, screening and transformations were handled.

body.text: Readers can only judge estimates if they know the data behind them (Appelbaum et al. 2018). Report:

items: Population, sampling procedure, period and response rate.
N collected and N analysed, with the reason for every exclusion; SEM Studio reports the number of cases used after listwise deletion.
Amount and pattern of missing data, the assumed [[missing-data-mechanism]] and the handling (listwise, FIML).
Item screening: reverse-scored items (with endpoints), dropped constant or problematic items, any other transformation.
Descriptive statistics of the indicators and the response scales with their endpoints.
Data provenance and licence, and clearly label synthetic or simulated data.

body.text: Justify the sample size with a power analysis for the smallest effect of interest. Simple rules such as "ten times the largest number of arrows pointing at a construct" are rough and are not a substitute for a power analysis (Hair et al. 2022).
SEM Studio keeps a transformation log in Data Lab and a method statement with every run; copy both into your notes before writing.

mistake.title: Reporting only the final N
mistake.text: Saying "N = 258" without mentioning that 242 of 500 cases were dropped for missing values hides a choice that can bias the results. Report N collected, N analysed and why they differ.

tryIt.task: Run this CFA with listwise deletion and read how many cases the result used and how many were dropped. Write one sentence reporting it.

checks.question: Your CB-SEM analysis used listwise deletion and kept 258 of 500 cases. What should the report state? Select all that apply.

options.text: That 500 cases were collected and 258 analysed after listwise deletion
options.feedback: Correct. Both numbers and the reason belong in the report.

options.text: The amount and pattern of missing values
options.feedback: Correct. Readers need it to judge whether listwise deletion was reasonable.

options.text: The assumption under which listwise deletion is unbiased (MCAR) and why it is plausible
options.feedback: Correct. Listwise deletion requires missingness to be completely at random.

options.text: Nothing; the analysed N is sufficient.
options.feedback: Hiding exclusions prevents readers from assessing bias and power.

checks.explanation: Transparency about the sample is a precondition for interpretation.

checks.question: A reviewer asks you to justify your sample size. Which answer is strongest?

options.text: A power analysis for the smallest effect of substantive interest, stating the assumed effect size, α and power.
options.feedback: Correct. It ties N to the effects you want to detect.

options.text: N exceeds ten times the largest number of arrows pointing at a construct.
options.feedback: This rule ignores effect sizes and reliability and is widely criticised as insufficient.

options.text: All paths were significant, so N was large enough.
options.feedback: Post-hoc significance does not justify N; non-significant paths would not show it was too small either.

checks.explanation: Plan N from the effects of interest.
